name: Flutamide
lead: Flutamide is a nonsteroidal antiandrogen: it occupies the androgen receptor so that testosterone and DHT have less effect on tissues such as the prostate, hair follicles and oil glands. It was the first drug of its type approved in the US, in 1989, for prostate cancer, and its labelled use is in combination with an LHRH agonist for locally confined and metastatic prostate carcinoma [1][2][15]. Its label carries a boxed warning for liver injury and says it is for use only in men [2].

For appearance, flutamide matters mainly in women. Off-label, it has been used for hirsutism (excess facial and body hair), acne, oily skin (seborrhea) and female pattern hair loss, where reducing androgen signalling in the follicle and sebaceous gland is the goal: less unwanted hair, clearer skin, and in some studies denser scalp hair [1][3][15]. Wikipedia's summary of the research describes studies in which women reported large reductions in acne and seborrhea scores and improved scalp hair, and notes that the drug has been used at doses well below those for prostate cancer [15]. A French review of antiandrogen treatments placed flutamide as third-line therapy for severe hirsutism, with no market authorisation for that use [3].

Because of the liver risk, newer guidance treats it as a later option. Reviews of androgenetic alopecia note that only finasteride and minoxidil are FDA-approved for the condition [5], and a Canadian consensus did not list flutamide among recommended interventions [9]. In online communities the drug turns up in hair-loss and androgen-receptor threads, mostly on T Nation, where members discuss it alongside other antiandrogens and compounds that affect androgen balance [11][13].
infobox: Oral (a topical gel is mentioned in forums)

paras: The US label indicates flutamide with LHRH agonists such as goserelin for stage B2-C prostate cancer, started before radiation, and for stage D2 metastatic carcinoma [2]. Earlier trials examined combined androgen blockade, including leuprolide with or without flutamide and orchiectomy with or without flutamide [6][7][14]; a 1990 review covers clinical applications of antiandrogens [8]. In prostate cancer, flutamide is given with a drug that lowers testosterone, because blocking the receptor alone raises circulating testosterone in men [15].

Flutamide has also been used in case reports to reduce spontaneous orgasms in men with post-orgasmic illness syndrome, and in endocrine conditions that involve high androgens in women, such as polycystic ovary syndrome and congenital adrenal hyperplasia [15].

Flutamide has been used off-label for hyperandrogenic skin and hair conditions in women, including hirsutism, acne, seborrhea and female pattern hair loss, because it blocks androgen action in follicles and sebaceous glands [1][15]. A review of antiandrogens ranks cyproterone acetate with an oral contraceptive first-line for moderate to severe hirsutism, spironolactone second-line, and flutamide or finasteride third-line [3]. A Canadian consensus on AGA did not list flutamide among interventions recommended [9].

Women who take it typically do so for months to years, and the studies describe benefits building over the first six to twelve months. Wikipedia notes that the related antiandrogen bicalutamide appears comparably effective for hirsutism with a much lower liver risk, which is one reason flutamide is now seldom a first choice [15].

Wikipedia reports that doses studied for hirsutism ranged widely and that trials found no significant difference in response across several lower daily doses, and that adding finasteride gave no extra benefit over flutamide alone [15]. Treatment is by specialists, with the drug prescribed off-label.

Wikipedia's review of the literature describes a long-term study of 230 women with acne, most with seborrhea, in which very-low-dose flutamide alone or with an oral contraceptive produced marked reductions after 6 months, with maximum effect around a year and benefits maintained in later years; 97 percent of the women reported being satisfied with acne control. Another study reported an 80 percent drop in acne and seborrhea scores in 3 months, against about 40 percent with spironolactone [15]. A topical-flutamide trial for acne vulgaris (50 participants) has also been registered and completed [16].

A general reference reports reductions of 50 to 70 percent in Ferriman-Gallwey scores after 6 to 12 months with low-dose flutamide in hirsutism studies [1]. Wikipedia describes the quality of evidence as moderate and notes effectiveness equivalent or superior to spironolactone, cyproterone acetate and finasteride in some comparisons, while stating that liver risk makes it less favoured [15].

In a study of 101 pre- and postmenopausal women, flutamide alone or with an oral contraceptive lowered hair-loss scores after a year, with maximum effect at two years and benefits maintained for two more; a small study reported cosmetically acceptable density gains in 6 of 7 women with diffuse thinning; and a comparative study found a 21 percent reduction in Ludwig scores after a year, where cyproterone acetate and finasteride had not helped [15]. For male pattern hair loss, no trials have been identified, and reviews of AGA and the Canadian consensus did not present flutamide as a standard option [5][9].

The boxed warning describes hospitalisation and rare deaths from liver failure, with about half of cases within the first three months, and recommends measuring transaminases before starting [2]. The label also warns of fetal toxicity and aniline-related toxicities including methemoglobinemia, hemolytic anemia and cholestatic jaundice [2]; methemoglobinemia has been reported in a case report [10]. Wikipedia reports that by 1996 there were 46 cases of severe cholestatic hepatitis with 20 deaths, and that a 2021 review found 15 serious liver cases in women treated with flutamide, including 7 transplants and 2 deaths [15].

In men, androgen deprivation brings hot flashes (over half of patients in a general reference), reduced libido, impotence, breast tenderness and gynecomastia, and diarrhea is more common than with bicalutamide [1][15]. In women the most common effect reported is dry skin, attributed to lower sebum production, and flutamide does not stop ovulation [15]. Rarer reports include interstitial pneumonitis, photosensitivity and neutropenia [15].
A T Nation poster in a 2009 thread on androgen-receptor hair loss said bicalutamide and flutamide carry more side effects orally, and that flutamide is recommended against [11].

The size of the liver risk is described differently across sources. A 1996 estimate based on prescriptions and MedWatch reports put serious hepatotoxicity near 3 in 10,000, while other work suggests the true figure could be higher; transient enzyme elevations are common, occurring in around 42 to 62 percent of men on treatment [15]. The proposed mechanism is mitochondrial toxicity linked to the nitroaromatic group, a feature absent from bicalutamide [15].

In the lower-dose regimens used in women, a 2009 controlled study of 214 women with hirsutism treated for a year, with liver enzymes checked at baseline and every three months, reported no AST or ALT elevations; the authors concluded long-term low-dose use appeared safe with enzyme monitoring [18]. Wikipedia also records a 2021 review of 15 serious liver cases in women, including 7 transplants and 2 deaths, so the literature contains both reassuring cohort data and documented severe injuries [15]. Monitoring of liver function is the standard recommendation [15][2].

Flutamide is a prodrug: its active form, hydroxyflutamide, binds the androgen receptor with roughly 10 to 25 times the affinity of the parent drug and competes with testosterone and DHT [15]. It is metabolised mainly by CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 with a half-life of about 6 hours, which is why it is taken several times a day [1][15]. It also weakly inhibits an enzyme (CYP17A1) involved in androgen synthesis, and it activates the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, which may be linked to liver toxicity [15]. Prostate cancer research has examined androgen-receptor mutations that arise under androgen antagonist treatment, including cases where flutamide can paradoxically stimulate the receptor [12][1].

Wikipedia notes that flutamide lowers PSA by roughly 75 percent in prostate cancer, compared with about 90 percent for bicalutamide, and that it was also used to blunt the transient testosterone 'flare' at the start of GnRH-agonist therapy [15]. In benign prostatic hyperplasia, a reduction in prostate volume of about 25 percent has been described, similar to finasteride, with breast tenderness and gynecomastia in about half of patients [15].

Flutamide was first synthesised in 1967 at Schering-Plough by Neri and colleagues, under the development code SCH-13521. It was originally investigated as an antibacterial agent, and its antiandrogen activity was discovered by chance [15]. Clinical research began in 1971 [15].

It reached the market in 1983 in Chile (as Drogenil) and West Germany (as Flugerel), and the US FDA approved it in 1989 for metastatic prostate cancer in combination with a GnRH analogue [15][1]. It was the first nonsteroidal antiandrogen; nilutamide followed in 1989 and bicalutamide in 1995 [15]. A 1989 New England Journal of Medicine trial of leuprolide with or without flutamide helped establish combined androgen blockade [6], and a later trial examined orchiectomy with or without flutamide [14].

Reports of liver injury accumulated through the 1990s; by 1996, 46 cases of severe cholestatic hepatitis with 20 deaths had been reported [15]. Newer agents, bicalutamide and enzalutamide, have largely replaced flutamide in prostate cancer because of better tolerability and once-daily dosing, though it remains on the WHO Essential Medicines List as an alternative [15].
The US brand is Eulexin; Wikipedia lists the original markets' names Drogenil (Chile) and Flugerel (West Germany), and capsules and tablets as the forms [2][15].

Discussion appears mainly on T Nation, where flutamide is mentioned with anabolic compounds and hair loss questions. A 2003 post advised that a prescription could give access to flutamide gel, described as better than topical spironolactone [13]. Posts in other threads mention it when discussing androgen-receptor blockers and side effects [4][11].
Flutamide is a prescription medicine in the US, sold as Eulexin, and its label restricts use to men with prostate cancer [2]. Use in women for skin and hair conditions is off-label [3].

Wikipedia summarises small studies in other fields: two phase II breast-cancer trials found few responses, and psychiatric work has covered bulimia nervosa and obsessive-compulsive disorder, with mixed results [15]. A registered phase 2 trial has examined androgen excess and fat-cell function in polycystic ovary syndrome [17].

Trials in prostate cancer are extensive, including combined androgen blockade trials with leuprolide and orchiectomy [6][7][14]. A 1990 review summarises clinical applications of antiandrogens [8]. For hirsutism in women, reviews summarise studies, with flutamide listed as third-line [3]. Registered trials include a completed topical flutamide study in 50 people with acne vulgaris and a phase 2 trial in women with polycystic ovary syndrome studying androgen excess and fat-cell function [16][17]. No published trial of flutamide for male pattern hair loss was identified.

lore.intro: Flutamide appears sparingly in forums as an antiandrogen, usually in hair-loss or androgen-receptor discussions on T Nation [11][13].

claims.claim: Topical flutamide is a stronger anti-hair-loss option than topical spironolactone.
claims.believers: A 2003 T Nation post said flutamide gel is far better than spironolactone [13].
claims.experts: No published trial of flutamide gel for scalp hair loss was found; reviews rank oral flutamide third-line for hirsutism [3].

claims.claim: Oral flutamide is a hair-loss option but carries more side effects than other antiandrogens.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster said bicalutamide and flutamide have more side effects orally and that flutamide is recommended against [11].
claims.experts: The label carries a boxed warning for severe and sometimes fatal liver injury [2].

claims.claim: Flutamide clears acne and oily skin faster than spironolactone.
claims.believers: Posters who discuss antiandrogens describe flutamide as the stronger blocker at the skin [13].
claims.experts: Wikipedia's review cites a study with an 80 percent drop in acne and seborrhea scores versus 40 percent for spironolactone, with the caveat of liver toxicity [15].

claims.claim: Low-dose flutamide in women is safe for the liver if monitored
claims.believers: Proponents of low-dose antiandrogen regimens for hirsutism and acne point to cohort data with no enzyme rises [18].
claims.experts: Wikipedia and case reports describe serious liver injuries, including transplants, in women, and labels carry a boxed warning [15][2].

claims.claim: Flutamide is a back-up when first-line antiandrogens have not helped hirsutism
claims.believers: Clinicians who prescribe it describe lower hair scores after 6 to 12 months of treatment [1].
claims.experts: A review ranks it third-line behind cyproterone acetate and spironolactone, and bicalutamide appears comparably effective with less liver risk [3][15].

card.summary: A prostate-cancer antiandrogen sometimes used off-label for female hirsutism and hair loss; liver toxicity makes it a last-line choice.
card.note: Boxed warning for liver failure; label says it is for men only.

quick.overview:
Flutamide is a prescription antiandrogen approved for prostate cancer. It has also been used off-label in women for excess hair growth, acne and hair thinning.
Evidence for scalp hair is thin, and guidelines rank it behind other antiandrogens because of liver risk.
quick.mechanism: It blocks androgen receptors, so testosterone and DHT have less effect on follicles and oil glands.
quick.risks: Boxed warning for severe, sometimes fatal liver injury; also fetal toxicity, methemoglobinemia, hot flashes and sexual side effects in men.

angle.text: In women, flutamide reduces androgen action in the skin and follicles, and studies describe lower acne and hirsutism scores and improved scalp hair. It is prescription-only and used off-label, usually under specialist supervision with liver monitoring.
